links.note: The quotation at the start of the chapter is Sri Aurobindo on the spiritual and cultural unity of the great surge of humanity between the Himalayas and the two seas, which this concept carries in full along with the map it sits beside.

What name you would have chosen for the country if you had been born some 2,000 years ago is verbatim one of the chapter's closing questions in this concept, and it is answered from the whole collection of ancient names rather than one of them.
Why people travelled to India from various parts of the world in ancient times, with a hint that there could be four or five motivations, is verbatim the last of this concept's closing questions.
How today's India differs from the India of the past - this concept states that the region has had many different names and shifting boundaries and was very different 500, 2,000 and 5,000 years ago.
Indian Subcontinent as the term for the region - this concept introduces it and then asks the reader to find its natural boundaries on the map.
The Rig Veda as India's most ancient text, which names the northwest region Sapta Sindhava - this concept's own sentence.
Sindhu referring to the Indus River, or at times to a river in general - this concept's gloss. Already linked and correct.
The Mahabharata listing Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga and Pragjyotisha - this concept's list of regions. Already linked and correct.
Bharata first appearing in the Rig Veda, where it refers to one of the main Vedic groups of people - this concept says so while explaining Bharatavarsha as the country of the Bharatas.
Jambudvipa meaning the island of the fruit of the jamun tree - this concept's gloss. Already linked and correct.

Ashoka, whose date we can take to be about 250 BCE, using Jambudvipa in an inscription to describe the whole of India - this concept's corroboration of the text by an inscription. Already linked and correct.
Jambudvipa in Ashoka's time including what is today Bangladesh and Pakistan as well as parts of Afghanistan - this concept's statement of its extent. Already linked and correct.

Cape Kumari in the south and the great mountain in the north come from the ancient Tamil poem quoted in this concept, which closes by remarking that it looks like ancient Indians knew their geography well.
The Constitution using India, that is Bharat at its beginning, with Bharat arthath India in the Hindi version - this concept's DON'T MISS OUT box. Already linked and correct.
The Persians, the ancient inhabitants of Iran, as the first foreigners to mention India, calling it Hind, Hidu or Hindu - this concept's opening.
Hind and Hindu as Persian adaptations of Sindhu - this concept states that the Persians gained control of the Indus region, earlier called Sindhu, and adapted the name into their own language.
The Greeks deriving Indoi and Indike from Persian sources, dropping the initial h because that letter did not exist in Greek - this concept's explanation.
The ancient Chinese referring to India as Yintu or Yindu, also derived from Sindhu - this concept's opening sentence.
Tianzhu also readable as heavenly master, reflecting Chinese respect for India as the land of the Buddha - this concept's point. Already linked and correct.
Xuanzang, who travelled from China to India in the 7th century CE, collected Buddhist texts and returned after 17 years - this concept's DON'T MISS OUT box. Already linked and correct.
Hindustan first used in a Persian inscription some 1,800 years ago - this concept's closing sentence. Already linked and correct.
Indike as the Greek pair to Indoi - this concept is where the ancient Greeks named the region Indoi or Indike, from which the English name descends.
Hind paired with the ancient Persians is the correct match, and this concept is where the Persians' earliest records and stone inscriptions refer to India as Hind, Hidu or Hindu.
The false pair is Sapta Sindhava as the land of seven seas; this concept gives it as the land of the seven rivers, which is what makes the option wrong.

The visible claim that Hindustan was first used by the British is judged against this concept, which says it was first used in a Persian inscription some 1,800 years ago and later became the term used by most invaders. Already linked and correct; the item's other numbered statements are missing from the stem.
The Sindhu or Indus as the river behind Hind, Indoi and ultimately India - this concept is the Persian-to-Greek chain the case describes. Already linked and correct.
Pragjyotisha as roughly today's Assam - one line of this concept's list of Mahabharata regions. Already linked and correct.
Ashoka's date taken to be about 250 BCE, which is what fixes a timeframe for the name Jambudvipa - this concept's reasoning. Already linked and correct.

The comparison rests on Sapta Sindhava naming only the northwest region of the subcontinent, which is this concept's statement; Bharatavarsha's wider extent is the contrast. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.
Ancient Chinese paired with Yintu is the correct match, and this concept is the one that gives Yintu and Yindu as the Chinese names for India.

The assertion that English India is a late development, evolving from earlier Persian and Sanskrit names for the Indus region, is this concept's chain - Sindhu to Hind or Hidu in Persian, then to Indoi or Indike in Greek.

Matching each name of India to the language it comes from, across Sanskrit, Persian, Greek and Chinese, is the table of the many names of India across seven languages that this concept's LET'S EXPLORE asks the reader to complete.

What the variety of names reflects about India's connections - this concept's summary is that names came both from ancient inhabitants and from foreign visitors to and invaders of India, which is the interaction the question asks about.
Sapta Sindhava as the land of the seven rivers - this concept's gloss, which is what makes flowing river systems the answer. Already linked and correct.
The jamun tree, also called jambul or Malabar plum, behind the name Jambudvipa - glossed in this concept. Already linked and correct.
Mahabharata paired with Bharatavarsha is the correct match, and this concept is where the Mahabharata is said to use the terms Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa.
The false pair is the ancient Greeks coining Bharatavarsha; this concept is where the Greeks' actual name, Indoi or Indike from Persian Hindu, is given, and where the Persians are credited with Hind.

The visible statement that Bharata appears in the Vishnu Purana is judged against this concept, which quotes the Vishnu Purana verse naming the country Bharata. The item's other numbered statements are missing from the stem.
The comparison turns on Hindustan's date, first used in a Persian inscription some 1,800 years ago, which this concept supplies. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.
The one true statement is that Xuanzang was a Chinese visitor, and this concept is the only one that describes him travelling from China to India in the 7th century CE.

A Persian report of the 6th century BCE about the land of Hidu refers to the Indus region - this concept dates the Persian campaign to the 6th century BCE and identifies Hidu with the Indus, earlier called Sindhu.

Foreign names originating from the Indus because it was the prominent feature met by those entering from the northwest - this concept is the mechanism, a foreign name for India being a foreign pronunciation of an Indian river.
What India, that is Bharat signifies about the country's identity - this concept is where the Constitution's phrase brings the ancient name into the present. Already linked and correct.
The Persians controlling the Indus region, which was earlier called Sindhu - this concept's sentence, in those words.

Setting Bharatavarsha as an Indian name against India and Hind as foreign ones is this concept's summary - the names given by ancient inhabitants include Jambudvipa and Bharata, while foreign visitors and invaders mostly adopted names derived from the Sindhu.

The snowy mountains of the Vishnu Purana's definition being the Himalayas - this concept quotes the verse, the country north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains, and asks the reader to identify them.

Matching India to Latin via Greek, Hind to Persian, Bharata to Sanskrit and spotting Indoi as not Chinese is the cross-language table of names this concept's LET'S EXPLORE builds, with Latin, English and French already filled in.
